To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the epidemic threshold in metapopulations is affected by the topologic fluctuations of the network and that the epidemic threshold is not a single value but rather a range of values that depend on the initial conditions.

the invasion threshold in heterogeneous metacommunities depends on the heterogeneity of the connectivity network, and is independent of the epidemic threshold, which is the same for homogeneous metacommunities.
the epidemic invasion threshold depends on the heterogeneity of the metapapulation network.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the interplay between diffusion and topology in the dynamics of epidemic processes.
the dynamics of epidemic processes and reaction-diffu- sion in heterogeneous metapopolulation networks.
the dynamics of susceptible-infected-recovered processes in metapopolation models.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the invasion threshold is a function of the network topology, and the mobility of the disease, which can be controlled by the mobility of the hosts.
the invasion threshold is a global property of the system, which depends only on the metapopulations' connectivity, and is independent of the details of the epidemic spreading process.
the metapopulations with heterogeneous connectivity patterns exhibit an invasion threshold, which is affected by the topologically induced fluctuations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the importance of the network topology for the invasion threshold in heterogeneous metacommunity networks.
the global invasion threshold is determined by a balance of the diffusion rate and the local epidemic threshold, and is affected by the fluctuations of the network.

the global invasion threshold is the key quantity that controls the spread of an infectious disease in a networked metapopulation, and it is a function of the topological properties of the network and of the diffusion rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the epidemic threshold is not only a function of the local epidemic dynamics but also depends on the global connectivity of the metapopolation network.
the invasion threshold can be lowered by increasing either the connectivity or the heterogeneity in the metapopulations network.
, in order to control an epidemic, it is necessary not only to reduce the mobility rate but also to reduce the topological fluctuations, i.e. to make the network more regular.
